paras: The lynching of an unnamed Black man near Millen, Georgia, took place in December 1882, when a mob overpowered the posse taking him to jail and killed him. He had been accused of attempting to assault a young white woman and had been bound over for trial. A Waynesboro letter in the Savannah Morning News and an Augusta wire dispatch reported the killing, and the wire carried it to papers across the country under headings such as "Lynch Law in Georgia."

According to the Waynesboro correspondent, the young woman, described as "highly respectable," was walking from her father's house to her brother-in-law's, half a mile away, when a Black man stopped her and tried to choke her. The accounts say he cut her twice across the breast, cutting through her clothes but not seriously injuring her, and fled when she called loudly for help. The Augusta dispatch added that she was going through the woods at the time.

The accused man was caught and bound over for trial. While a posse, called "the officers" in the wire version, was taking him to jail, a mob overpowered his guards and seized him. The Savannah correspondent wrote that he was "disposed of by Judge Lynch," and the wire reports said only that he was lynched. A later summary in a Minnesota weekly was the only report to say that he was hanged.
None of the reports names the man, the woman, the members of the posse, or anyone in the mob, and none says where or at what hour he was killed.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of mob members, or any official response appears in the coverage, which ended within about ten days.

The earliest report came from a correspondent signing himself "M.," whose Waynesboro letter of December 19 appeared in the Savannah Morning News on December 21 between items on a county fair and an artesian well. Its subheading read "A Negro Fiend Lynched," and the letter called the accused a "wretch" and treated the lynching in the familiar phrase "Judge Lynch" without criticism.

An Augusta dispatch dated December 22 carried the story north and west, appearing on December 22 and 23 in papers in Yankton, Portland, Sacramento, St. Paul, New York, Lancaster, Washington and Knoxville. The fuller version ran under headlines such as "A Negro Miscreant Lynched" in the New-York Tribune and "Lynch Law in Georgia" in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, while a one-sentence version appeared in crime columns headed "Negro Lynched" or "LYNCHED." These papers reprinted the dispatch without comment, repeating its description of the accused as a "miscreant."

Weekly news digests in Kentucky, Minnesota, New Hampshire and elsewhere condensed the story further through December 30, sometimes changing its details. The collection has no Black-press coverage from this period.

The reports disagree on the date: the Waynesboro letter put the attempted assault on December 18 and the lynching on December 19, while wire derivatives placed events on "Thursday," December 21, and one summary dated the hanging "the 22d." Because the letter was written locally and printed before the Augusta dispatch was sent, it is the earlier evidence for the date.

The town also varies: the local letter and the fuller dispatch say Millen, while shorter versions printed Nelson, Wilton or Milton. One Kentucky summary said the mob took him "from jail," against every other report that he was seized on the way there.

reader.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man near Millen, Georgia (1882)
bases: A mob took a Black man accused of an attempted assault from the posse or officers taking him to jail and lynched him (A1, A7, A9).

Every account says he was 'lynched' or 'disposed of by Judge Lynch' after a mob overpowered the posse taking him to jail (A1, A6, A9); the killing punished an alleged attempted outrage on a white girl before trial (A1, A7).

A Waynesboro correspondent's letter (A1) and the separate Augusta wire dispatch (A6, A7, A9) agree on the accusation, the arrest, and the seizure and lynching on the way to jail, though they differ on dates and the town name.

accounts.label: Waynesboro correspondent
accounts.gist: Wrote on Dec. 19 that the attempt happened the day before and that he had 'incidentally learned' of the lynching at Millen that day; the posse taking the man to jail was overpowered and he was 'disposed of by Judge Lynch.'

accounts.label: Augusta wire (full)
accounts.gist: Dated Dec. 22; repeated the woodland walk, the two cuts and the arrest, and said a mob took him from the officers on the way to jail and lynched him.

accounts.label: Augusta wire (short)
accounts.gist: One sentence placing the attempt 'near Nelson' and saying he was taken from the officers on the way to jail and lynched.

accounts.label: Weekly summaries
accounts.gist: Later briefs said he was 'taken from jail by a mob' or 'hanged by a mob at Nelson, Ga., on the 22d.'

framing.detail: The Georgia letter headed the item 'A Negro Fiend Lynched,' called him a 'wretch' and the woman 'highly respectable,' and used the jocular 'disposed of by Judge Lynch.'
Northern and western papers ran the Augusta wire under 'A Negro Miscreant Lynched,' 'Lynch Law in Georgia,' 'Negro Lynched' or in crime columns, without comment.

conflicts.note: The Waynesboro letter is dated Dec. 19 and was printed Dec. 21, before the Augusta wire's Dec. 22 dateline, so it is the earlier and more local evidence; the later dates appear to be read from the wire dateline.
The local letter and the fuller wire text both say Millen; the other names appear only in short wire derivatives and are likely transmission errors.

record_check.dossier: The Dec. 19 Waynesboro letter reports the lynching 'to-day' (1882-12-19); Dec. 21-22 come only from the Augusta wire and its derivatives.
No report names a county; the local account is datelined Waynesboro.
Seizure and lynching are reported throughout; hanging appears only in one later Minnesota summary.
Millen is supported by the local letter and the fuller wire; Nelson, Wilton and Milton are wire variants.
Supported: seized from the posse or officers on the way to jail (one summary says from jail).
